title: Pair Programming Interview Format
summary: How a live pairing round differs from solo coding rounds: shared control, an existing codebase, and genuine back-and-forth collaboration.

slides.markdown:
A solo whiteboard round tests whether you can produce a correct algorithm under pressure, alone. A **pairing round** tests something different and arguably closer to the actual job: can you build with someone else, inside code you didn't write, while thinking out loud.

Candidates who ace solo coding sometimes stumble here because they treat it like a solo round with an audience — heads-down, silent, defending every choice. This topic covers how pairing rounds are typically run, what's evaluated beyond correctness, and how to work inside an existing codebase and negotiate who drives.

slides.sectionTitle: How pairing rounds are typically run: driver/navigator, an existing repo
slides.markdown:
Most pairing interviews use the **driver/navigator** model borrowed from real pair programming: one person types (the driver), the other reads, questions, and suggests direction (the navigator). You'll usually start as driver on someone else's existing repository — a small service or app the interviewer already knows well — rather than a blank file.

The task is typically a feature addition or bug fix scoped to 30-45 minutes, not a from-scratch algorithm problem. That framing matters: you're being dropped into an unfamiliar codebase under time pressure, which is exactly what a first week on a new team feels like.

Expect the interviewer to swap roles partway through, or to ask you to swap — that's normal, not a sign you're doing something wrong.

slides.sectionTitle: What's evaluated beyond correctness: collaboration and adaptability
slides.markdown:
A correct, working solution is necessary but nowhere near sufficient in a pairing round. Interviewers are watching for **how you collaborate**: do you explain your reasoning before typing, do you actually listen when the interviewer suggests a different direction, do you ask about unfamiliar code instead of guessing?

They're also watching **adaptability** — how you react when a suggestion contradicts your plan, or when you realize you misunderstood the existing code. A candidate who calmly adjusts reads as far stronger than one who ships the technically-correct answer while ignoring every cue from their partner.

In practice this means: a slightly slower solution built collaboratively usually scores higher than a faster solo-style solution built while tuning out the interviewer.

slides.sectionTitle: Working inside someone else's codebase and conventions
slides.markdown:
Dropped into an unfamiliar repo, your first instinct should be orientation, not action: skim the file structure, find how existing tests are written, and notice naming and formatting conventions before adding a single line. Matching the existing style — even if you'd structure it differently on a green-field project — signals you know how to work inside a team's codebase rather than rewriting it to your taste.

If you spot something you'd genuinely refactor, name it out loud rather than silently changing it: "I notice this function does two things — should I split it as part of this change, or keep scope tight and just note it?" That question itself is a strong signal; silently refactoring unrelated code eats your limited time and can look like you're avoiding the actual task.

When you're unsure how something works, ask rather than guess — the interviewer usually knows the code and would rather answer a question than watch you debug a wrong assumption for five minutes.

slides.sectionTitle: Negotiating who drives and when to swap
slides.markdown:
If the interviewer doesn't assign roles explicitly, it's fine — and often expected — to propose one: "I'll drive first since I want to get oriented in the code, feel free to jump in." Waiting silently for someone else to decide wastes time and can read as passive.

Watch for natural swap points: after finishing a discrete sub-task, when you're stuck and the interviewer has an idea, or around the halfway mark if no swap has happened yet. Offering to swap ("want to drive the next part?") shows you see pairing as genuinely shared, not just narrated solo work.

If you're the navigator, stay actively engaged rather than going quiet — suggest, question, catch mistakes. A silent navigator gives the interviewer nothing to evaluate during that half of the round.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: how a typical pairing round is timed
slides.markdown:
A common shape is a **45-60 minute** slot: 5 minutes of orientation and small talk, 5-10 minutes getting oriented in the codebase and clarifying the task, 30-40 minutes of actual building (often with one role swap), and 5 minutes to wrap up and discuss what you'd do next.

Knowing this shape helps you self-pace: if you're still reading files at minute 20, you're behind, and it's worth saying so out loud — "let's make sure we leave time to actually implement something; I think I have enough context, should we start?" That kind of time-awareness itself reads as a positive signal, since it's exactly what you'd do managing a real ticket against a deadline.

Don't expect to finish a "complete" feature — most tasks are scoped knowing full completion isn't the point; a partial, well-reasoned implementation with a clear plan for the rest is a normal, successful outcome.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: solo whiteboard coding vs pairing round expectations
slides.markdown:
The two formats reward different behavior, and applying whiteboard habits to a pairing round is a common miscalibration.

| | Solo whiteboard | Pairing round |
|---|---|---|
| Primary signal | Algorithmic correctness, complexity analysis | Collaboration, adaptability, working in existing code |
| Silence | Neutral or expected while thinking | A negative signal — narration is expected throughout |
| Disagreement | Rarely happens — no one to disagree with | Expected and welcomed when handled well |
| Finishing the task | Usually necessary to pass | Often unnecessary if the process was strong |
| Codebase | Blank file, your own conventions | Existing repo, someone else's conventions to respect |

**How to decide your approach:** if you catch yourself going quiet and heads-down the way you would solo, that's the signal to consciously switch modes back to narrating and checking in.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: steamrolling the interviewer's suggestions instead of collaborating
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I know the right approach, so I should push through it even if the interviewer suggests something else."

**Why it's wrong:** the interviewer's suggestion is often a deliberate probe — they may be testing whether you can incorporate feedback, or they may genuinely know something about the codebase you don't yet. Dismissing it outright, talking over it, or visibly ignoring it and continuing your own plan reads as poor collaboration regardless of whether your original approach was technically sound.

**Correct model:** treat every suggestion as worth a genuine beat of consideration — "that's a good point, let me think about how that changes this" — even if you end up sticking with your approach after explaining why. The response matters more than which approach wins.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior-level nuance: shaping scope out loud when the task is underspecified
slides.markdown:
A junior candidate in a pairing round takes the task as given and tries to implement exactly what was said. A senior candidate notices when the task itself is underspecified and shapes it out loud before diving in — "before I start, should this handle the case where the list is empty, or is that out of scope for this round?"

This mirrors real work: a staff engineer handed a vague ticket doesn't just start typing, they clarify scope with whoever assigned it, in front of the person who can answer. Doing this in a pairing round, live, with the interviewer as your stand-in product owner, is one of the clearest signals of seniority the format can surface — more than raw typing speed or algorithm choice ever will be.

The same instinct — checking scope with a collaborator before committing time — pairs naturally with [why-code-review-and-what-to-look-for](why-code-review-and-what-to-look-for), where catching this kind of ambiguity is exactly what a good reviewer does after the fact.
